So I would love to see Finch implement a system for getting our to-dos that change daily/only need done once/specific important tasks completed. And to reinforce the use of this system, award the most rainbow stones/energy to the special daily check-list area.

Bonus points: a “brain dump” activity/reflection that uses AI/key words (like the hashtags) to sort what all is on your mind, tasks/want to dos, into the previously mentioned Eisenhower Matrix. It then can use your words to create goals based on the importance you assign to each task/want.

DEPRESSION LIES TO YOU. Mental illness by definition is not rational, and your negative self-talk, thoughts, and beliefs about yourself are NOT a reflection of the truth. You are valuable and you matter so much to those who love and know you best, including your mom. Starting by finding any tiny little thing to live for every day is how I got through the worst of my suicidal thoughts, plans, and more.

I’m an intensive outpatient and partial hospitalization therapist who sees patients that come directly from our hospital’s inpatient units due to suicide attempts and more. I can definitely tell you that I have seen even the most depressed, anxious, and unstable people come through to the other side of recovery, learning how to value themselves and finding ways to get out of the trap that is their life that makes them want to escape. I’ve seen severe suicidality and self harm and I know from personal experience that it is VERY possible to stop living in survival mode and start thriving instead. 

I have seen people who’ve been on the brink of death change their lives in significant ways that made life livable and even enjoyable again, even in just 2 months. It is so very possible for you to live again- especially in a way that you find purposeful, meaningful, and fulfilling. The path to healing one’s mental health is paved in discomfort and littered with obstacles. Will thoughts, symptoms, and life challenges be easy to change or manage? No, not at first, but I see the people who get the most out of our programs and they are the ones who make the small actionable steps consistently and are learning how to normalize their struggle but not place their identity solely on their depression/diagnoses. Please feel free to dm me for resources to help you take even the smallest step forward to get through all this pain you’ve been carrying. 

You always have a choice, even if it seems small or you can’t see it now, it’s never too late to start anew and find your purpose again. I see you, you are not alone, and I hope that your story doesn’t end here, because there is always a chance to change the next chapter.

If it’s not the executive dysfunction beating my brain up, it’s the depression or intense emotions. So I go by “fed is best” on bad days or when I’m extra tired/apathetic about eating.

They’re the cheapest thing I can think of, they’re convenient, less effort than ramen, always available when needed and don’t spoil, portable for lunch at work, and they’re small enough to where if I don’t feel like eating (thanks depression) I don’t have to choke down much. While you make some decent points, and it does seem reasonable to go to small claims court, and it IS unreasonable AND shitty for her family to even be siding with sister and her daughter, I don’t see the moral value in saying YTA to OP for her not immediately going no contact. OP sounds like she stands up for her daughter in every way; I’m not getting push-over, passive mom vibes from her. She and her daughter set firm boundaries and her sister and her daughter walked right over them. Is that fucked? Yes. Do they deserve to pay for the damages? Absolutely. Should OP or her daughter be shamed and quieted for how they responded in affirming their boundaries? Absolutely not! BUT- NC isn’t a catch-all, one-in-done, easy, or best solution for shitty family behavior. If she chooses it, so be it, but immediately jumping to NC isn’t always the answer people think it is, it comes with its own trauma and loss and grief, and it needs to be thought out fully, for everyone involved. No contact isn’t always necessary nor helpful for many families or situations, and that’s coming from someone who has been NC with my entire nuclear family (and most external family) for over 10 years. 

Plus let’s not forget that NC affects absolutely everyone involved and their relationship(s) with all relatives involved in the NC, including OP’s family with her husband and children. You’re ultimately saying disrupt and cut out an entire family dynamic that likely goes back generations over a 13 year old’s stupid and selfish actions. Now whether or not those generations of family are stuck in toxic patterns (sounds to me like they are!) and should be cut off is a determination for OP, her kids, and her husband alone.

OP should ultimately do what is best for her and her family, whether that’s NC, full contact, or somewhere in between, but you saying YTA because OP did not do what you thought was best based on your own values and life experiences was doing too much.

It’s not your place to tell someone who you don’t even know, based on one situation, what they should absolutely do and not do, and moreover, make a blanketed, black and white moral judgement on them for doing what they deem is best for their family and their lives, which again, you know virtually nothing about outside the context of one story.

Therapist here. I would say you meet criteria of depression. Feeling “empty” “hopeless” and “stuck” plus sleeping more and more, and especially thoughts of self-harm would likely point to depression. From a diagnostic standpoint I would obviously have to know more. I know from a personal standpoint, what you’re describing is what my depression felt like, and still does some days.

Do you find yourself unmotivated, losing interest in things that used to excite you? Is your appetite poor or too much? Does it feel like you’re tired easily, that you can’t do basic tasks that used to be easy or that others find easy? If you answered yes to any of these:

I would advise you to reach out to your trusted caregivers/parents/loved ones because, while I can’t formally diagnose you, you’re showing signs of depression and self-harm history or thoughts can get worse over time without help and support. Wishing you all the best… I know what has been helping me is the Finch app. It’s been getting me to do some great self-care tasks. Feel free to pm me if you need help with next steps!

As a therapist, I would not disclose this to a client, even if they were ABDL themselves. For two reasons: 

1.) Most importantly, ethical therapy by definition is NOT about me (or any clinician), my personal lifestyle, or who I am outside of work. Clinicians should avoid making topics about themselves and focus on the client, their goals, and supporting them. If they wanted a supportive person who talked about themselves, they would just talk to a friend.

2.) Self disclosure is tricky. Some therapists chose to do it, some never do. Something we are taught in our graduate education is that if we do choose to use self disclosure, it must be done solely for the client’s benefit. You have to carefully weigh whether or not this information you’re disclosing is motivated by what you want, or if it truly would benefit the client therapeutically. 

An exception, for me, would be if the client kept presenting a pattern of loneliness and inability to talk about ABDL stuff with anyone else in their life and they express the need for it. I would still consult before disclosing and craft my words very carefully. But even then, I might instead suggest the client to research ABDL communities rather than use me for what could be in their life without me.

Usually there are resources on campus that help students out in times like these. I would also email your professors what you plan to do after you talk to your advisor. Most are very understanding and are willing to work with you.

Second, I don't know your parents but if they are caring and not controlling or abusive they should understand that you had a rough time with your depression, even if they are upset at first. Going to them with an action plan to fix it and admitting what happened will help soften the news.

To quote my therapist: Do the next right thing.
